Summary tables from a survey design

Source: vignettes/articles/survey-tables.Rmd
survey-tables.Rmd

A sample that is stratified, clustered, weighted to a population or carried by replicate weights is not a simple random sample. Its mean is still a weighted mean. The standard error depends on the strata and the clusters, the degrees of freedom count sampling units and not rows, and the tests are corrected for the design. A column of weights does not carry that information.

spicy has three functions for these samples: table_continuous_svy(), table_categorical_svy() and table_battery_svy(). They compute nothing themselves. Every number comes from the survey package (Lumley, 2004, 2010), and spicy adds what its other tables have: the same columns, the same outputs and the same typed view, with a note that says which design produced the numbers.

library(spicy)
library(survey)
data(api)

Three designs from survey’s own api data, used throughout:

dclus1 <- svydesign(id = ~dnum, weights = ~pw, data = apiclus1, fpc = ~fpc)
dstrat <- svydesign(
  id = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, data = apistrat, fpc = ~fpc
)
rclus1 <- as.svrepdesign(dclus1)

Continuous variables 

table_continuous_svy(dclus1, select = c(api00, api99))
#> Descriptive statistics
#> 
#>                                                             95% CI              
#>                                                       ──────────────────        
#>  Variable   │    M         SD       Min       Max        LL        UL       n   
#> ────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  api00      │  644.17    105.75    411.00    905.00    593.68    694.66    183  
#>  api99      │  606.98    112.85    365.00    890.00    555.02    658.94    183  
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 14 degrees of freedom. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit.

After the sample size, three sentences of the note describe the design. It is a one-stage cluster sample of 15 school districts with a finite population correction. The standard errors come from Taylor linearization. The interval is a t interval on 14 degrees of freedom, the number of clusters minus one. The 183 schools do not enter that count.

confint() on a survey object uses the normal distribution by default:

m <- svymean(~api00, dclus1)
confint(m)                    # survey's default: normal
#>          2.5 %   97.5 %
#> api00 598.0275 690.3113
confint(m, df = degf(dclus1)) # what the table reports
#>          2.5 %   97.5 %
#> api00 593.6763 694.6625

svyciprop(), svyquantile(), svyttest() and regTermTest() take their degrees of freedom from the design, and so do the tables. Each spends them as its statistic requires: svyttest() uses one on the estimated difference, so its t has degf(design) - 1 degrees of freedom, 13 here. The note gives the number.

Choosing the statistics

show_columns takes the tokens of table_continuous(), with "se" (the design-based standard error) and "deff" (the design effect) added and "med_ci" removed. The columns follow the order of the tokens:

table_continuous_svy(
  dclus1,
  select = api00,
  show_columns = c("m", "se", "ci", "med_iqr", "n", "weighted_n", "deff"),
  deff = TRUE
)
#> Descriptive statistics
#> 
#>                                95% CI                                   
#>                            ──────────────                               
#>  Variable │   M      SE      LL      UL         Mdn [Q1, Q3]         n  
#> ──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  api00    │ 644.17  23.54  593.68  694.66  652.00 [552.00, 719.00]  183 
#> 
#>  Variable │ Weighted n  DEff 
#> ──────────┼──────────────────
#>  api00    │  6194.00    9.35 
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 14 degrees of freedom. Quantiles: Hyndman-Fan type 1. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. SE = design-based standard error of the mean; CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit; Q1 = first quartile; Q3 = third quartile; DEff = design effect.

The design effect is 9.35: the variance of this cluster sample is nine times that of a simple random sample of 183 schools. A table that ignored the design would report a standard error three times too small.

"med_ci" is refused. The exact interval of table_continuous() inverts a binomial sign test, and its coverage rests on independent observations, which a clustered or stratified sample does not have. For a design-based interval on the population median, call survey::svyquantile(interval.type = ) on the design.

Groups

by = cuts one domain per group. survey recomputes the degrees of freedom on the sampling units each domain retains, so a grouped table generally carries a different df per row, and the note gives their range:

table_continuous_svy(dclus1, select = api00, by = stype, statistic = TRUE)
#> Descriptive statistics by stype
#> 
#>                                                        95% CI          
#>                                                    ──────────────      
#>  Variable │ Group    M       SD     Min     Max      LL      UL     n  
#> ──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  api00    │ E      648.87  106.16  436.00  905.00  600.91  696.83  144 
#>           │ H      618.57   96.74  443.00  724.00  528.67  708.48   14 
#>           │ M      631.44  109.06  411.00  847.00  561.87  701.01   25 
#> 
#>  Variable │ Group       Test         p   
#> ──────────┼──────────────────────────────
#>  api00    │ E      F(2, 12) = 1.28  .314 
#>           │ H                            
#>           │ M                            
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; degrees of freedom vary by group (7–14). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. P-value: design-based Wald test. The group comparison uses 12 degrees of freedom (observed groups only). CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit.

The comparison is a single design-based test on the whole design: svyttest() with two observed groups, the Wald F of regTermTest() with three or more, and svyranktest() under test = "nonparametric". Under a design the variance is that of the design, and the distinction between the Welch and the Student test does not exist. test = "student" warns and behaves like the default.

The intervals use those degrees of freedom. svyby(vartype = "ci") builds its interval with confint.default(), on a normal quantile, and returns a narrower interval than the tables here. The two differ by the ratio of qt(0.975, degf(design)) to qnorm(0.975): the interval of the table is 9% wider on the 14 degrees of freedom of dclus1.

Categorical variables 

table_categorical_svy(dclus1, select = c(stype, awards))
#> Categorical table
#> 
#>  Variable   │   n      %    
#> ────────────┼───────────────
#>  stype      │               
#>    E        │  144    78.7  
#>    H        │   14     7.7  
#>    M        │   25    13.7  
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  awards     │               
#>    No       │   53    29.0  
#>    Yes      │  130    71.0  
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 14 degrees of freedom. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. % = estimated percentage. n = observed (unweighted) count.

n is the observed count: 144 schools of type E were sampled. The 78.7% beside it is an estimate of the share in the population. The table shows both, and the note gives the estimated population (6194) beside the sample size (183).

table_categorical_svy(
  dclus1,
  select = stype,
  proportion_ci = TRUE,
  deff = TRUE
)
#> Categorical table
#> 
#>                                  95% CI             
#>                              ──────────────         
#>  Variable   │   n      %       LL      UL     DEff  
#> ────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────
#>  stype      │                                       
#>    E        │  144    78.7    67.1    87.0    2.40  
#>    H        │   14     7.7     3.5    15.8    1.91  
#>    M        │   25    13.7     8.4    21.3    1.40  
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 14 degrees of freedom. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. Percentage CIs: Wald on the logit scale (logistic regression). % = estimated percentage. n = observed (unweighted) count. CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit; DEff = design effect.

The percentage comes from svymean() and the interval from svyciprop(). svyciprop() estimates on the transformed scale of its method, and a percentage taken from it would change with ci_method, in the thirteenth decimal. ci_method is a property of the interval, and the proportion should not depend on it.

table_categorical_svy(dclus1, select = stype, by = sch.wide)
#> Categorical table by sch.wide
#> 
#>                    No            Yes           Total             
#>               ────────────  ─────────────  ─────────────         
#>  Variable   │  n      %       n      %       n      %       p    
#> ────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  stype      │                                              .022  
#>    E        │  12    52.2    132    82.5    144    78.7          
#>    H        │   3    13.0     11     6.9     14     7.7          
#>    M        │   8    34.8     17    10.6     25    13.7          
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Percentages are column percentages. Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; degrees of freedom vary by group (9–14). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. P-value: design-based Pearson chi-squared (Rao-Scott second-order correction). % = estimated percentage. n = observed (unweighted) count.

The p is svychisq(): Pearson’s chi-square with the Rao-Scott second-order correction, referred to F(ndf, degf(design)). chisq_statistic offers "Chisq", "Wald", "adjWald" and "saddlepoint" as well. Two of survey’s seven are refused: "lincom", whose numerical integration ?pchisqsum documents as failing when the upper tail approaches machine epsilon, and "wls-score", which has no reporting convention here.

The association measures of table_categorical() (Cramér’s V, phi, tau-b and tau-c, gamma, Somers’ D, lambda) are not offered. None has an established design-based variance, and the intervals table_categorical() gives them assume simple random sampling. The table reports the design-based test in the p column. For an effect size, fit a model: table_regression(survey::svyglm(...)).

Item batteries

table_battery_svy() is the design twin of table_battery(): several items answered on one scale, one row per item and one column per level.

table_battery_svy(
  dclus1,
  select = c(awards, sch.wide, comp.imp, both),
  by = stype
)
#> Item battery by stype
#> 
#>                    E               H               M              
#>             ───────────────  ──────────────  ──────────────       
#>  Variable │  No   Yes    n    No   Yes   n    No   Yes   n    p   
#> ──────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  awards   │ 22.9  77.1  144  57.1  42.9  14  48.0  52.0  25  .075 
#>  sch.wide │  8.3  91.7  144  21.4  78.6  14  32.0  68.0  25  .075 
#>  comp.imp │ 22.2  77.8  144  50.0  50.0  14  44.0  56.0  25  .123 
#>  both     │ 22.2  77.8  144  50.0  50.0  14  44.0  56.0  25  .123 
#> 
#> Note. Design: cluster (dnum), 15 PSUs, with finite population correction; 14 degrees of freedom. Percentages are row percentages estimated under the design. Base: respondents who answered the item. Item p-values, each item by group: design-based Pearson chi-squared (Rao-Scott second-order correction). Adjusted for 4 tests (Holm method). n = observed (unweighted) count.

The base of a row is the schools that answered the item, n their observed count, and each percentage is svymean() on that domain. Each item is tested against stype by svychisq(), Rao-Scott corrected, and the four p-values are adjusted together by Holm’s method.

A stratum with one sampling unit

A stratum with a single primary sampling unit has no variance to estimate, and under its default options(survey.lonely.psu = "fail") survey stops there, point estimate included. The table is still produced, with a dash in each cell survey could not estimate and a sentence of the note that says what the dash means. The function also warns, once, quoting survey’s message. Here the one school left in stratum H falls in the No group of sch.wide, so the other group is estimated as usual:

keep <- c(which(apistrat$stype != "H"), which(apistrat$stype == "H")[1])
lonely <- svydesign(
  id = ~1, strata = ~stype, weights = ~pw, data = apistrat[keep, ]
)
table_continuous_svy(lonely, select = api00, by = sch.wide)
#> Warning in table_continuous_svy(lonely, select = api00, by = sch.wide): Some cells could not be estimated:
#> • `survey::svyttest()`, `survey::svymean()`, `survey::svyvar()` stopped: "Stratum (H) has only one PSU at stage 1"
#> ℹ The cells that could not be estimated show a dash.
#> ℹ A stratum has a single primary sampling unit, which stops survey under its default `options(survey.lonely.psu = "fail")`: "adjust", "average", "remove" or "certainty" estimate these cells (see `?survey::surveyoptions`).
#> Descriptive statistics by sch.wide
#> 
#>                                                        95% CI             
#>                                                    ──────────────         
#>  Variable │ Group    M       SD     Min     Max      LL      UL     n   p 
#> ──────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  api00    │ No        –       –    398.00  778.00     –       –     25  – 
#>           │ Yes    678.42  121.28  421.00  893.00  655.85  700.99  126    
#> 
#> Note. N = 151 (weighted 5454). Design: stratified (stype); degrees of freedom vary by group (22–124). A dash marks an estimate the design could not provide: a stratum has a single primary sampling unit. Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit.

The values "adjust", "average", "remove" and "certainty" of that option let survey estimate these cells, each by its own convention (?survey::surveyoptions), and the table then follows them. A warning of survey’s own, such as the one on a stratum with a single primary sampling unit in a domain under options(survey.adjust.domain.lonely = TRUE), is said once per table, with the number of times survey raised it.

Replicate weights

A replicate-weights design goes through the same functions. The point estimates depend on the weights alone and are identical. The standard errors come from the replicates and differ:

table_continuous_svy(rclus1, select = api00)
#> Descriptive statistics
#> 
#>                                                             95% CI              
#>                                                       ──────────────────        
#>  Variable   │    M         SD       Min       Max        LL        UL       n   
#> ────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  api00      │  644.17    105.75    411.00    905.00    587.70    700.64    183  
#> 
#> Note. N = 183 (weighted 6194). Design: replicate weights (JK1), 15 replicates; 14 degrees of freedom. Std. errors: design-based (replicate weights, JK1). Confidence intervals and tests use the design degrees of freedom. CI = confidence interval; LL = lower limit; UL = upper limit.

Weights, or a design?

table_continuous(weights = ) and table_continuous_svy() read a weight differently, and they do not estimate the same standard deviation.

table_continuous(weights = ) follows the frequency-expansion convention: a weight is a number of copies, and SD has denominator sum(w) - 1. With integer weights the statistics are those of the data repeated that many times.

table_continuous_svy() follows the sampling-weight convention: a weight is a number of units represented, and SD is sqrt(survey::svyvar()), whose denominator is n - 1 on weights normalized to sum to n.

rescale = TRUE makes the two agree, by an identity. With w' = w * n / sum(w), so that sum(w') = n:

sum(w' (x - xbar)^2) / (sum(w') - 1)
  = (n / sum(w)) * sum(w (x - xbar)^2) / (n - 1)
  = n / (n - 1) * sum(w (x - xbar)^2) / sum(w)

and the right-hand side is what survey::svyvar() computes. On a design that declares nothing but weights, the two tables agree:

d_iid <- svydesign(id = ~1, weights = ~pw, data = apiclus1)

svy <- table_continuous_svy(d_iid, select = api00, output = "long")
wtd <- table_continuous(
  apiclus1, select = api00, weights = pw, rescale = TRUE, output = "long"
)
c(svy = svy$sd, weighted_rescaled = wtd$sd)
#>               svy weighted_rescaled 
#>          105.7489          105.7489

Under the default rescale = FALSE they differ, each following its convention:

expanded <- table_continuous(
  apiclus1, select = api00, weights = pw, output = "long"
)
c(svy = svy$sd, weighted_default = expanded$sd)
#>              svy weighted_default 
#>         105.7489         105.4681

The mean is the same under both conventions: sum(w x) / sum(w) does not change when the weights are rescaled.

A design carries more than weights. On the cluster design, the same mean has a standard error that the weights alone do not give:

c(
  iid_design = table_continuous_svy(d_iid, select = api00, output = "long")$se,
  cluster_design = table_continuous_svy(dclus1, select = api00, output = "long")$se
)
#>     iid_design cluster_design 
#>       7.817181      23.542241

Passing a design to table_continuous(), or a data frame to table_continuous_svy(), is an error that names the other function.

Regression under a design

table_regression() reads a fit of survey::svyglm(), survey::svyolr() or survey::svycoxph(), on a linearized or a replicate-weights design. The coefficients, the variance and the degrees of freedom all come from survey.

gl <- svyglm(api00 ~ ell + meals + stype, design = dstrat)
table_regression(gl)
#> Survey-weighted linear regression: api00
#> 
#>  Variable    │    B      SE          95% CI          p   
#> ─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept) │  865.99   8.54  [ 849.16,  882.83]  <.001 
#>  ell         │   -0.56   0.34  [  -1.24,    0.12]   .104 
#>  meals       │   -3.43   0.24  [  -3.90,   -2.96]  <.001 
#>  stype:      │                                           
#>    E (ref.)  │     –      –            –            –    
#>    H         │ -128.29  10.40  [-148.81, -107.78]  <.001 
#>    M         │  -60.46   9.76  [ -79.72,  -41.20]  <.001 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n           │  200                                      
#>  Weighted n  │ 6194                                      
#>  AIC         │ 2197.8                                    
#> 
#> Note. Survey-weighted linear regression. Design: stratified (stype), with finite population correction; 193 residual degrees of freedom. AIC of a design-based fit: design-based AIC (dAIC). Std. errors: design-based (Taylor linearization). CI = confidence interval; AIC = Akaike information criterion.

The note states the design and the residual degrees of freedom of the tests, and it names the variance estimator. The fit statistics give the observed n and the Weighted n the estimates describe, the pair the descriptive tables print in their note.

Regression tables for survey designs covers these models: the degrees of freedom, weights compared with a declared design, odds ratios and average marginal effects, the tests of a term, subpopulations, replicate weights, ordinal and Cox fits, and what a design-based fit refuses.

Quantiles

qrule chooses the rule, and the note names the one in force. The default "math" estimates the quantile of the population, inf{x : F(x) >= p}. "spicy" switches to the type-7 interpolation of table_continuous(), for a reader who needs the two tables to agree cell for cell. Any other value, a function included, is passed to survey::svyquantile() as it is.

q <- function(rule) {
  table_continuous_svy(
    dclus1, select = api00, qrule = rule,
    show_columns = c("med", "q1", "q3"), output = "long"
  )[, c("q1", "median", "q3")]
}
rbind(math = q("math"), spicy = q("spicy"), hf7 = q("hf7"))
#>          q1 median  q3
#> math  552.0    652 719
#> spicy 552.0    652 719
#> hf7   552.5    652 718

Downstream

These tables carry the typed view the rest of the package uses, so as_structured() and inline() work as they do elsewhere:

tbl <- table_categorical_svy(dclus1, select = stype, by = sch.wide)
s <- as_structured(tbl)
s$body[, c("Variable", "Yes n", "Yes %", "p", ".row_role")]
#>   Variable Yes n  Yes %          p     .row_role
#> 1    stype    NA     NA 0.02174746 factor_header
#> 2        E   132 82.500         NA         level
#> 3        H    11  6.875         NA         level
#> 4        M    17 10.625         NA         level
names(s$spanners)
#> [1] "No"    "Yes"   "Total"
inline(tbl, "stype", level = "E", column = "pct", model = "Yes")
#> [1] "82.5"
inline(tbl, "stype", column = "p")
#> [1] ".022"

Rendering

Every engine of the family is available: "tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "word", "excel", "clipboard", plus "data.frame" for the displayed table with its numbers and "long" for one row per variable, level and group.

table_continuous_svy(
  dstrat,
  select = c(api00, api99),
  by = stype,
  output = "gt"
)

What is not here yet

Two-phase, pps, database-backed and multiframe designs are refused with a classed error. The delegation to survey was verified on svydesign() and as.svrepdesign() designs only. Call survey directly for the others. If one of them matters for your work, open an issue on the tracker of the package and name the design.

References

  • Lumley, T. (2004). Analysis of complex survey samples. Journal of Statistical Software, 9(8), 1–19.
  • Lumley, T. (2010). Complex surveys: A guide to analysis using R. John Wiley & Sons.
